title: A Pilot Study of Medical Misinformation Perceptions and Training Among Practitioners in North Carolina (USA)
screen_reason: Online survey of 2,183 licensed physicians and physician assistants in North Carolina (May 2020) reporting the share who say patients raised medical misinformation in a clinical encounter in the past year (94.2%), plus topic-specific shares reporting 'often' or 'sometimes' encountering misinformation. These are self-reported encounter shares with stated denominators, i.e. RECALL (exposure). Note the exposure is to misinformation voiced by patients in consultations, not to media content.

estimates.platform: Face-to-face clinical encounters (not a media platform)
estimates.date: Survey fielded over 3 weeks in May 2020; recall window the previous year
estimates.measure_type: % of licensed practitioners who report that a patient raised medical misinformation in a clinical encounter within the past year
estimates.denominator: 2,183 eligible respondents (licensed physicians and physician assistants currently practising in North Carolina) out of 2,889 unique responses and 24,571 practitioners invited
estimates.definition: Respondent answered yes to whether patients had raised medical misinformation in a clinical encounter within the past year, judged against the survey's supplied definition
estimates.misinfo_def: "information that is factually inaccurate or not supported by current evidence-based medical literature and/or practices"
estimates.source_quote: such experience is almost universal among our respondents, with 94.2% reporting encounters with patient MM within the previous year.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 3; restated in Abstract and Discussion
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Practitioner self-report and recall. The survey supplied its own definition of medical misinformation because, as the authors note in Limitations, licensing boards and medical societies have no standard definition. Respondents judged for themselves what counted.
estimates.moderator_quote: We received permission to administer the survey to all licensed practitioners in the state of North Carolina from the North Carolina Medical Board (NCMB) and contacted practitioners via email. … The response rate was 8.9% (2183/24 571).
estimates.notes: borderline=true on scope, not on the number: this is exposure to misinformation voiced BY PATIENTS in face-to-face consultations, reported by clinicians — interpersonal, second-hand, professional-population exposure, not audience exposure to media content. It sits at the edge of an audience-exposure review and is easy to mis-pool with population media-exposure figures; population_scope=professional and platform_norm=other flag it. INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY: Table 3 reports the same numerator 2047 as 98% of 2,089 responses (and 1,975, 95%, of 2,081 in the formal-training row), whereas the Results text gives 2047/2183 = 94.2%. The text figure is used. Severe non-response: 8.9% response rate, and the authors concede likely participation bias by interest in the topic. Fielded during the May 2020 COVID lockdown.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) TWO TOPIC ROWS DELIBERATELY NOT EXTRACTED — statins and alternative cancer therapy. Table 1 gives the four frequency categories (statins: often 508 (24%), sometimes 530 (25%), of 2,089; alternative cancer therapy: often 226 (11%), sometimes 609 (29%), of 2,100) but the paper never states the combined 'often or sometimes' share for these two, unlike the four topics it does state. Producing them would require a cross-category sum, which R8 forbids. For reference only, they would be ~49.7% and ~39.8%. (2) SPECIALTY SUBGROUPS (Table 2) not extracted per the subgroup rule: encounter rates ranged 86% (radiology) to 100% (endocrinology), with a Table 2 total of 2,043 (94%) of 2,169 — a third slightly different denominator for the same headline quantity. (3) DENOMINATOR INCONSISTENCY worth an adjudicator's eye: the same 2,047 who reported an encounter appear as 94.2% of 2,183 in the Results text and as 98% of 2,089 in Table 3; Table 3's formal-training row gives yet another pair, 1,975 (95%) of 2,081. The abstract also contains an obvious typo, '39% (807/289)', for 807/2,089. (4) Training figures (formal 18%, 380/2,081; informal 39%, 807/2,089) are exposure to TRAINING, not to misinformation — no row. (5) No content, behavioural or platform data of any kind; nothing to support CONTENT, EXPOSURE, REACH, SHARING or CONCENTRATION rows.

rob.design: Anonymous cross-sectional online survey (RedCap, 22 questions) of physicians and physician assistants licensed by the North Carolina Medical Board, fielded over three weeks in May 2020 during the state COVID-19 lockdown; reported per CHERRIES. 24,571 invited by email, 2,889 unique responses, 2,183 analysed after removing largely incomplete responses and practitioners not currently practising in NC — a response rate of 8.9%. Partially complete responses accepted, so item denominators vary (2,081–2,183). No compensation, no weighting, no probability sampling. Misinformation was defined by the investigators because no standard definition exists from licensing boards; all measures rest on respondent perception and recall. Authors flag non-response, likely topic-interest participation bias, and undelivered invitations routed through institutional administrative staff. Chi-square used for specialty comparisons was invalid due to small 'no' cells and Fisher's exact did not converge, so the specialty comparison is presented without a p-value. 95% CIs reported for the pooled proportions.
rob.item6_quote: In the survey, we defined MM as "information that is factually inaccurate or not supported by current evidence-based medical literature and/or practices."
rob.item10_quote: When asked if patients had raised MM in a clinical encounter within the past year, 94.2% (2047/2183) of respondents said yes.
